title: Ethiopian Lamb Tibs
community: All of Ethiopia — lamb as the celebration protein
author: Chef Haile
desc: Ethiopian Lamb Tibs — the celebration version of tibs using young lamb, cooked fast and hot in kibbeh with jalapeños, rosemary, onions, and tomatoes. Lamb tibs is served at the most important Ethiopian celebrations — weddings, Christmas, Easter, and Timkat.
longDesc: Lamb tibs is the tibs of celebration — more expensive, more tender, and more flavourful than beef tibs. Young Ethiopian highland lamb has a mild sweetness that pairs magnificently with the kibbeh and berbere. Served at weddings and religious celebrations, it signals the generosity of the host.
ingredients: 600g young lamb — leg or shoulder, cubed 2cm
equipment: Cast iron pan or clay shekla pot
steps: Sear lamb in a single layer — 2 minutes per side.
Add tomatoes, berbere, pepper, and salt.
Lamb should be medium — pink in the centre.
chefTips: Young lamb — under 1 year old — is essential for tenderness and mild flavour.
Lamb tibs should be slightly pinker than beef tibs — do not over-cook.
The rosemary and lamb combination is one of the great flavour pairings in Ethiopian cooking.
commonMistakes: Using old lamb — strong and tough.
cookingScience: Young lamb has significantly less myoglobin than older animals — producing the characteristic pale pink colour and milder flavour. The fat in young lamb is primarily subcutaneous rather than intramuscular, melting quickly in the hot kibbeh and contributing to the sauce richness.
sustainabilityTips: Ethiopian highland lamb — grass-fed on highland pastures.
healthBenefits: Young lamb is leaner than beef.
culturalNote: Lamb tibs at an Ethiopian celebration is a mark of honour — the host who serves lamb tibs is saying 'you are worth the finest food we can offer'. At Ethiopian weddings, the lamb slaughtered for the feast is done so at dawn, and the tibs served by midday represents the full cycle of Ethiopian hospitality.
